title: Dissociation of NaCl in supercritical aqueous fluids of moderate and high concentrations: A molecular dynamics study
authors: Mikhail V. Ivanov, Olga V. Alexandrovich
abstract: We report classical molecular dynamics simulations of NaCl association and dissociation in supercritical aqueous fluids over a wide range of salt concentrations, from moderate salinity to highly concentrated H2O-NaCl mixtures attainable at high temperatures. The degree of dissociation a and the corresponding ideal dissociation constant Kd, derived directly from a, were calculated as functions of the stoichiometric NaCl mole fraction at selected pressure-temperature (PT) conditions from 673.15 to 1273.15 K and from 0.1 to 2 GPa. At moderate salinity corresponding to a molality of approximately 1 mol/kg, NaCl remains largely dissociated a = 0.3-0.7 depending on pressure and temperature). In contrast, when the mole fraction of NaCl increases up to xNaCl = 0.333 (27.8 mol/kg), the degree of dissociation tends towards zero, and most ions form Na$^+$Cl$^-$ contact pairs and multi-ion clusters. As a result of these competing trends, the mole fraction of structurally dissociated Na$^+$ and Cl$^-$ ions is a non-monotonic function of the stoichiometric NaCl concentration and typically reaches a maximum at xNaCl = 0.06-0.10. This result shows that increasing salinity does not necessarily increase the abundance of structurally available chloride ions in supercritical aqueous fluids. Additional fixed density simulations at 1 and 7 mol/kg extend the analysis up to 1673.15 K and separate the effects of temperature and density on the associate/dissociate state of the ions. The obtained concentration dependences provide molecular-level constraints for thermodynamic descriptions of concentrated supercritical electrolytes and for evaluating chloride availability in high-temperature aqueous fluids.
summary: This study uses Molecular Dynamics simulations to map out how salt dissociation occurs in supercritical water under varying temperature, pressure, and salinity. The key finding is that increasing salt concentration does not guarantee higher ion availability because strong ion pairing and clustering dominate at high concentrations. This provides crucial molecular data for developing accurate thermodynamic models of concentrated electrolytes.
main_problem: The study investigates how the degree of dissociation ($\alpha$) of NaCl changes as a function of salt concentration in supercritical aqueous fluids, challenging the assumption that higher salinity always means more free ions.
main_result: The mole fraction of structurally dissociated $	ext{Na}^+$ and $	ext{Cl}^-$ ions is non-monotonic with increasing salt concentration, peaking at low concentrations ($	ext{x}_{	ext{NaCl}} \approx 0.06–0.10$), indicating that high salinity leads to ion pairing/clustering.
method: Classical Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations were employed using established force fields and thermostats to model the fluid behavior across wide ranges of temperature, pressure, and composition.
model_or_system: The system is an $	ext{H}_2	ext{O–NaCl}$ mixture simulated in supercritical conditions. The water is modeled by the flexible SPC/fw potential, and ion interactions use the Smith–Dang force field within a periodic boundary condition framework.
key_observables: Degree of dissociation ($\alpha$), ideal dissociation constant ($K_d$), average coordination number ($n_q$), and mole fraction of dissociated ions ($	ext{x}_{	ext{Cl}^-}$).
important_parameters: Temperature range: $673.15$ to $1273.15 	ext{ K}$; Pressure range: $0.1$ to $2 	ext{ GPa}$; Concentration: From moderate ($\approx 1 	ext{ mol/kg}$) to high ($x_{	ext{NaCl}} = 0.333$).
main_assumptions: The use of classical MD simulations is necessary due to computational constraints, and the definition of 'dissociated' relies on geometric criteria (e.g., distance $r > q$) rather than solely thermodynamic equilibrium.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of $\alpha$ and $\log_{10}K_d$ on salt concentration ($x_{	ext{NaCl}}$), showing a rapid decrease at high concentrations, and also show trends related to pressure and density.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the effect of varying $P$, $T$, and $x_{	ext{NaCl}}$ on ion association. It first establishes the simulation methodology, then presents results demonstrating that dissociation is limited by clustering effects at high salt loads, concluding with molecular constraints for thermodynamic models.
why_interesting: While not directly quantum mechanical, this work addresses complex many-body interactions and phase behavior in extreme conditions, which informs the development of accurate statistical mechanics models required for understanding highly dense or non-ideal systems.
